description: We are Students from United International University, BRAC University, and American International University-Bangladesh. We work in applied AI, computer vision, and full-stack development with React and FastAPI. Our focus is usability: turning NASA open data into a tool a person can act on in seconds, not a dashboard someone has to study.
summary: PolarWindow is a free web application that assists mission teams in planning lunar south pole landings. Near the lunar south pole, the Sun and Earth remain at low elevation angles. Consequently, a single topographic feature can obstruct solar illumination or radio communication for multiple days. A lunar lander requires solar illumination for electrical power. It also requires direct line of sight to Earth for telemetry and communication. PolarWindow uses NASA lunar elevation maps and planetary ephemeris data, meaning calculated positions of celestial bodies. At hourly intervals, the model computes when each candidate site maintains visibility of the Sun and Earth. For any selected site and time window, the interface reports four metrics: sunlight hours, Earth contact hours, longest night, and longest period without Earth contact. Each metric displays its data source and its margin of error. The platform also tracks every NASA commercial lunar delivery across sequential mission stages. Mission teams can define custom missions and evaluate alternative parameter scenarios. An artificial intelligence (AI) assistant answers user queries in accessible language using only internally computed metrics. The application never ranks or selects an optimal landing site. Instead, the interface presents the computed data, and the mission planner makes the selection.
details:
PolarWindow assists mission teams in selecting landing sites and dates near the lunar south pole. For any selected site and time window, the system computes four metrics. The first two metrics are total hours of sunlight and total hours of Earth contact. The remaining two metrics are the longest night and the longest period without Earth contact. Each value displays its data source and its margin of error. The platform also tracks every NASA Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) delivery through six stages. These stages are Ready, Launch, Trip, Surface, Contact, and Return. Mission teams can add custom missions and test alternative parameter scenarios. An integrated artificial intelligence (AI) assistant answers questions in accessible language.

How it works
The calculation begins with NASA laser elevation maps of the lunar south pole. These maps come from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) aboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). For each site, the system computes the horizon profile, meaning the elevation outline of surrounding terrain. NASA's SPICE, meaning Spacecraft, Planet, Instrument, C-matrix, Events data, provides Sun and Earth positions at any moment. At hourly intervals, the model checks whether the Sun and Earth remain above that horizon profile. Summing these hourly states produces the four visibility metrics. The illumination estimates were validated against NASA's reference illumination maps. The trajectory model was also validated against four completed lander missions. Those missions are IM-1, IM-2, Blue Ghost 1, and Peregrine. The AI assistant invokes only the application's internal computation tools. An output filter blocks any response containing numbers not returned by those tools.

Who it helps
Lander and payload teams can evaluate candidate sites and launch dates within a single interface. Students and the public can track lunar landings without specialized software. NASA's planetary datasets are publicly available, but they are distributed across multiple archives. PolarWindow consolidates these datasets and presents them in accessible language. Informed site selection can extend both solar power generation and Earth communication duration.

Tools we used
The system is implemented in Python, TypeScript, and SQL. The backend uses FastAPI, NumPy, PostgreSQL, Redis, and SpiceyPy, a wrapper for NASA's SPICE toolkit. The frontend uses React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and three.js. Automated testing uses pytest, Vitest, and Playwright. The test suite comprises 1,797 tests, all of which pass. The application is deployed in Docker containers on Google Cloud. Client access requires no specialized hardware and functions across desktop and mobile web browsers.

What makes it creative
PolarWindow does not assign composite scores or rank candidate landing sites. Instead, the interface presents the computed metrics, and the mission planner makes the selection. When a parameter is unavailable in public records, the interface labels it "not published". Estimated values display a striped pattern to distinguish them from measured data. Each mission stage is classified as archival record, worked example, or user-input required. The AI assistant also displays the derivation trace for each response.

What we thought about
Data verifiability was the primary design constraint, requiring a source and error margin for every metric. Accessible terminology allows mission planners to use the interface without prior training. Deployment on a single small cloud server minimizes operational cost. Responsive layout design supports both mobile phones and laptop computers.

Impact and the UN Sustainable Development Goals
PolarWindow aligns with three United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals. Goal 9 addresses Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure. The platform provides small lunar enterprises with a free mission-planning tool. Comparable analysis software is currently restricted largely to major space agencies. Goal 4 addresses Quality Education. Students can examine observational NASA data and observe how lunar landings are planned. Because each metric documents its derivation, the platform also functions as an instructional resource. Goal 17 addresses Partnerships for the Goals. PolarWindow relies exclusively on open datasets from NASA and other public repositories. The source code is open source, permitting independent verification, reuse, and extension. Shared access enables space teams across countries to operate from a common evidence base.

Other impacts
Loss of electrical power or telemetry contact can terminate a lander mission prematurely. Evaluating candidate sites in advance can prevent multi-year delays and substantial financial loss. These visibility constraints also apply to crewed Artemis missions targeting the lunar south pole. In addition, PolarWindow makes lunar mission analysis accessible to the public. Users can monitor a commercial delivery from launch through surface operations. The architecture also demonstrates a verifiable method for combining AI with scientific data. The AI assistant cannot fabricate numerical values and exposes each calculation step. Finally, the application runs on a single small server, which minimizes energy consumption.

How we used AI

Claude Code assisted in drafting and reviewing source code, test suites, and documentation. The development team verified all generated artifacts and retains full responsibility for them. Google Gemini generated five short video clips and twelve schematic illustrations. Google Gemini also powers Ask, the in-application assistant. Ask can report only numerical values returned by the application's internal tools.
